sentences.text: The attic light had been left on for as long as anyone could remember, and nobody could say who had done it.
It bothered Ines more than it bothered anybody else.
She had asked her uncle about it twice.
The first time he had said it was cheaper than arguing about it, which was not an answer.
The second time he had said that some things in a house are older than the people in it, which was less of an answer than the first one but sounded more like one.
She could see it at night from the garden — a thin orange line around the edge of the trapdoor, hanging in the dark of the landing ceiling like a picture of a door rather than a door.
She went up on the first warm night of the year, because the trapdoor had begun to hum.
That was new.
It was a low sound, not electrical, more like the noise a bee makes inside a jam jar three rooms away.
It had started on the Tuesday and by the Friday she could feel it in the ladder rungs.
She waited until her uncle had gone out to lock the greenhouse, and then she went up.
The attic was full of moths.
Not fluttering.
Not knocking themselves stupid against the bulb, which is what moths do and the only thing Ines had ever seen them do.
These were resting.
Hundreds of them, folded flat against the rafters and the underside of the roof slates, wings closed, absolutely still, arranged the way pages are arranged in a book.
They were the colour of old paper — some almost white, some the yellow of a page that has been in a window, a few nearly brown.
They did not startle when her head came up through the hatch.
One near her hand adjusted itself very slightly, the way a person shifts in a chair.
She sat on the edge of the hatch with her legs down through it, because the floor did not look trustworthy, and she looked at the one nearest to her.
There was something on its wings.
Not a pattern.
She knew what moth patterns looked like: eyes and speckles and the little false faces.
This was a picture.
A very small one, painted in the way a stamp is printed, right across both wings so that the join ran through the middle of it.
It was a kitchen.
A yellow kitchen with a window over the sink and a chair pulled out from the table.
She looked at the next one.
A boat, on a grey sea, seen from behind.
She looked at the next one, and it was a face she almost knew, and then did not, and the almost stayed with her all the way down the ladder.
